channel.title: Reasoned Talk
channel.description: This podcast shares my research into the legal histories of China and the West. Episodes follow cases, institutions, and legal ideas to ask how power is exercised, how people seek justice, and how law can hold rulers to account.
channel.itunes:author: Mason Hu

item.title: 04 Little Cabbage: The Failure of Justice in Late-Qing China
item.description:
In 1873, the death of a tofu-shop worker in eastern China became a poisoning case against his wife and their former landlord. Torture produced confessions, and repeated reviews upheld the accusation.

Following the woman remembered as Little Cabbage, this episode asks how official accountability could discourage correction, and why family petitions, elite connections, newspaper coverage, and central intervention were needed to reopen the evidence.

The eventual reversal saved two lives, but exposed how unevenly access to justice was distributed.

Hi, I'm Mason Hu, a lawyer in China. This is Reasoned Talk, a podcast about legal history in China and the West.

Key dates

  • November 1873: Ge Pinlian dies in Yuhang, near Hangzhou. His mother's request for an investigation leads to a poisoning accusation against his wife and their former landlord, Yang Naiwu.

  • January 1877: Officials from the Ministry of Punishments have Ge's remains examined at Haihui Temple in Beijing. The examiners conclude that he died of illness rather than poison.

  • 1877: The murder accusation is overturned, and officials involved in the case are punished or dismissed. Bi still receives a penalty for conduct judged improper; Yang's examination status is not restored.

Terms and names

  • Yang Naiwu (杨乃武) — A recently successful provincial examination candidate accused of helping poison Ge Pinlian. His examination status was revoked before he was subjected to torture and confessed.

  • Bi Xiugu (毕秀姑) — Ge's wife and the other accused person, better known as Little Cabbage. Contemporary official records call her 葛毕氏, a married designation identifying her birth surname as Bi. Her personal name varies in later accounts.

  • Little Cabbage (小白菜; Xiao Baicai) — Bi's nickname, traditionally explained through her fair complexion and white-and-green clothing. The gossip about “a sheep eating cabbage” plays on Yang's surname sounding like the Mandarin word for sheep.

  • Ge Pinlian (葛品连) — The tofu-shop worker whose death set the case in motion. The final official investigation attributed his death to illness; the episode does not identify a specific modern diagnosis.

  • Liu Xitong (刘锡彤); Chen Lu (陈鲁) — The Yuhang county magistrate and Hangzhou prefect, respectively. Their examination and interrogation of the accused shaped the original poisoning case.

  • Yang Changjun (杨昌浚) — The governor of Zhejiang who endorsed the proposed death sentences after provincial review. He is a different person from Yang Naiwu.

  • Yang Juzhen (杨菊贞); Madam Zhan (詹氏) — Yang Naiwu's elder sister and wife, who helped sustain the petitions challenging the case.

  • Hu Xueyan (胡雪岩); Xia Tongshan (夏同善) — A wealthy merchant and a senior official associated with support for the Yang family's campaign. Later accounts describe Hu's financial assistance; Xia helped the effort to secure central review.

  • Juren (举人) — The status awarded for passing the provincial civil-service examination. It brought social standing and procedural privileges, including protection against ordinary judicial torture while that status remained in force.

  • Ministry of Punishments (刑部); Censorate (都察院) — Central institutions responsible for criminal review and scrutiny of official misconduct, respectively. The ministry ultimately reinvestigated this case; the Censorate was one channel for complaints against provincial officials.

  • Capital petition (京控; jingkong) — A petition to central authorities in Beijing. “Capital” refers to the seat of government. Such petitions could be returned to the province for further proceedings.

  • Confession-centered justice; judicial torture — Confessions carried great weight in Qing criminal procedure. The law permitted specified forms of physical coercion while also setting limits; coercion could produce an account that appeared to confirm an official's assumptions.

  • Official accountability for wrongful judgments — Rules penalizing wrongful decisions, inaccurate examinations, and careless adjudication. Penalties depended on the conduct involved. In this case, fear of exposure could give reviewers a shared interest in defending an earlier decision.

  • Lingchi (凌迟) — Execution by slicing, the punishment proposed for Bi in the provincial proceedings.

  • The Washing Away of Wrongs (洗冤录) — The conventional English title associated with a Chinese forensic tradition reaching back to Song Ci's thirteenth-century work. The Qing official handbook belonged to a later version of that tradition.

  • Shenbao (申报) — A Chinese-language newspaper published in Shanghai that followed the case over several years. Its coverage circulated petitions and challenges to the official account beyond the locality where the case began.

Sources and reading

  • An English-language reconstruction: William P. Alford, “Of Arsenic and Old Laws: Looking Anew at Criminal Justice in Late Imperial China”, California Law Review 72 (1984), starting at p. 1180, especially sections II–III and Appendix A. Reconstructs the case from official records, diaries, and contemporary reporting, and discusses the reliability of different accounts. Older spellings include Yang Nai-wu, Hsiao-pai-ts'ai, and Shen Pao.

  • The official findings and proposed punishments: Ministry of Punishments, Final memorial on the Ge Pinlian case (光绪三年二月刑部定案奏折) (1877). This online transcription records coercion, alterations to the file, and the final recommendations. It distinguishes the unproved murder and adultery accusations from the remaining penalties. The official claim that the prisoners' injuries had healed differs from later accounts of lasting injury. The examiners' interpretation of bone color is a historical finding, not a modern toxicological demonstration.

  • Review, petitions, and interrogation: Draft History of Qing, volume 144, Treatise on Penal Law III (清史稿·刑法志三), particularly the sections on capital review, capital petitions, examinations, and interrogation. This later institutional history provides context for the procedures. The annual Autumn Assizes principally concerned death sentences held over for further review; not every capital case followed an identical sequence of hearings.

  • Supporters, political connections, and the press: Lu Yongdi (陆永棣), “落日残照：晚清杨乃武案昭雪的历史、社会与制度因素”, Peking University Law Journal / 中外法学, no. 4 (2007), pp. 31–60; PDF, especially PDF pp. 12–15 and 20–22. Examines the networks supporting the petitions and Shenbao's role. Some details of Hu Xueyan's assistance come from later recollections. Lu calls Bi 毕生姑, or Bi Shenggu, illustrating the variation in accounts of her personal name.

  • Why a dark silver needle does not establish arsenic poisoning: “砒霜——亦敌亦友，千年情仇”, University Chemistry / 大学化学 (2019), section 1.2. Explains silver's reaction with sulfur impurities in some historical arsenic preparations. A dark needle is not a specific test for arsenic, even if the prescribed washing procedure is followed.

item.title: 03 Trump vs. Birthright Citizenship: Court Fight Isn't Over
item.description:
Donald Trump lost his bid to restrict birthright citizenship at the Supreme Court in June 2026. In August, he signed another executive order. By September, families were suing again in Nathan v. Trump. Why does the fight continue after the Court has ruled?

Starting with Trump's renewed challenge, this episode examines the legal battle behind Trump v. CASA, the class-action response, and the six-to-three decision in Trump v. Barbara. The constitutional arguments reach back to Reconstruction and Wong Kim Ark, the American-born son of Chinese immigrants whose citizenship the government refused to recognize. Five justices backed the constitutional guarantee in Barbara; a sixth rejected the order on statutory grounds. Their disagreement helps explain what Trump can still try, what the Constitution protects, and why families may need to return to court to enforce it.

Hi, I'm Mason Hu, a lawyer in China. This is Reasoned Talk, a podcast about legal history in China and the West.

Key dates

  • 1857: Dred Scott v. Sandford denies federal constitutional citizenship to the class of people of African descent described in the decision, including free descendants of enslaved people.

  • 1866: Congress enacts the Civil Rights Act of 1866, including a statutory citizenship provision.

  • 1868: The Fourteenth Amendment constitutionalizes a citizenship guarantee and overturns Dred Scott's citizenship rule.

  • 1895: Wong Kim Ark is refused entry at San Francisco after a visit to China.

  • March 28, 1898: United States v. Wong Kim Ark is decided, 6–2.

  • January 20, 2025: Trump signs Executive Order 14160. Its section 2 sets out the two parental-status categories and its prospective application.

  • June 27, 2025: Trump v. CASA limits universal injunctive relief without deciding the citizenship order's substantive legality. Barbara v. Trump is filed the same day.

  • July 10, 2025: The New Hampshire district court provisionally certifies a nationwide class of affected children and issues a class injunction, stayed for seven days to allow appellate review. The certified class excludes parents and uses births on or after February 20, 2025.

  • April 1, 2026: The Supreme Court hears argument in Trump v. Barbara.

  • June 30, 2026: The Court affirms the district court. Six justices vote against the executive order; five join the constitutional holding. Kavanaugh relies on the statute for the result and expressly rejects the constitutional holding.

  • August 6, 2026: Trump signs Executive Order 14418, claiming to identify additional categories outside the birthright-citizenship rule recognized in Barbara.

  • August 11 and September 9, 2026: Plaintiffs' counsel announce further motions concerning a subsequent executive order. These entries identify litigation activity, not adjudicated outcomes.

  • September 28, 2026: Nathan v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03377, is filed in the District of Columbia, challenging the August order and implementing agency actions. A new complaint is not a new constitutional ruling.

Sources and reading

  • The constitutional text: National Archives, The Constitution: Amendments 11–27, Amendment XIV, sections 1 and 5. The Script paraphrases the citizenship sentence and quotes only its jurisdiction qualification.

  • Dred Scott: Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. (19 How.) 393 (1857), especially the citizenship ruling and denial of federal jurisdiction. The scope is described in relation to the class identified in the opinion; the episode does not equate the decision with a holding that every person of every African background had identical circumstances.

  • Wong's circumstances and the 1898 holding: United States v. Wong Kim Ark, 169 U.S. 649 (1898), especially pp. 652–653, 674–675, 682, 693, and 705. The agreed record identifies his 1873 birth, his parents' permanent domicile, his 1895 return, and their lack of diplomatic employment. The script separates those facts from later disagreement about how broadly the reasoning applies. Chinese exclusion and racial naturalization restrictions are not described as already in force at his birth.

  • What the order actually directs: Executive Order 14160, “Protecting the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship”, January 20, 2025, 90 Fed. Reg. 8449, especially sections 2–3. Both categories retain the specified condition concerning the father. The order's date is distinguished from its Federal Register publication on January 29. Its recognition and documentation directions are distinguished from a lawful amendment of constitutional citizenship.

  • CASA and the limits of interim relief: Trump v. CASA, Inc., Nos. 24A884, 24A885, and 24A886, June 27, 2025. See Barrett's opinion, especially slip pp. 1–5, 19, 21–24, and 26, and Sotomayor's dissent. The Court addressed the likely limits of equitable authority conferred by the Judiciary Act, partially stayed relief exceeding what plaintiffs required, and did not decide the order's merits. The script avoids saying citizenship actually became different from state to state as an automatic result of CASA.

  • The representative procedure: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23, especially subdivisions (a), (b)(2), and (c). The four general prerequisites and the additional basis for classwide injunctive relief are both relevant.

  • The class definition and injunction: Barbara v. Trump, No. 1:25-cv-00244-JL-AJ, Document 65, D.N.H., July 10, 2025, especially printed pp. 9–11 and 36–38. This is the district court's order, reproduced by Justia. The proposed class included parents; the certified class did not. The order uses February 20, 2025, as the first date of birth and provides a seven-day stay.

  • The substantive decision and separate opinions: Trump v. Barbara, No. 25-365, 609 U.S. ___ (2026), argued April 1 and decided June 30, 2026. Roberts's opinion occupies PDF pages 6–31 (slip pp. 1–26); Jackson's concurrence, PDF pages 32–51; Kavanaugh's opinion, PDF pages 52–61; Thomas's dissent, PDF pages 62–152; Alito's dissent, PDF pages 153–191; Gorsuch's dissent, PDF pages 192–194. Page numbering restarts for each opinion. Kavanaugh's slip p. 1 expressly rejects the constitutional holding while finding a statutory violation. Jackson's concurrence discusses Reconstruction and caste; the three dissents are characterized by their legal arguments, without adopting their historical conclusions as settled fact. The procedural posture remains review of preliminary relief, even though the Supreme Court resolves the constitutional issue.

  • The separate statutory protection: 8 U.S.C. § 1401, especially subsection (a), with subsection (b) relevant to the historical tribal-citizenship distinction. The script does not suggest that Congress can override Barbara's constitutional holding merely by amending this provision.

  • The post-decision requests: ACLU, August 11, 2026 announcement and September 9, 2026 announcement. These are statements by counsel for the plaintiffs, used in the timeline to identify their requests for clarification and a new class. Their characterizations of the order's legality are not presented as a subsequent judicial holding, and these announcements do not establish the latest docket status.

  • Trump's renewed order: Executive Order 14418, “Continuing To Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship”, August 6, 2026, especially sections 1–2. Section 2(b)(iv), read with section 2's condition that neither parent is a citizen, supplies the international-organization example in the closing. The order claims to implement exceptions within Barbara; the script identifies that as the administration's position, not an authoritative interpretation of the Supreme Court's holding. This example does not summarize every category in the order.

  • The new case used in the opening: Nathan v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-03377, Document 1, D.D.C., filed September 28, 2026, especially paragraphs 6–10, 29, 43, 49–50, and 94–102, and the requested relief. The complaint challenges the new order and implementing actions under the Fourteenth Amendment and 8 U.S.C. § 1401. Its treatment of the diplomatic exception and international-organization employment is attributed to the challengers. It is evidence of their claims and filing, not a judicial finding that the new order is unlawful. See also the filing docket reproduced by Justia and counsel's case summary for the withdrawal of the requests in Barbara and filing of a separate action in Washington. The script identifies a recent new lawsuit and makes no claim that no other litigation activity occurred afterward.

item.title: 02 A Son's Revenge: Filial Duty and the Law in Tang China
item.description:
In late seventh-century China, Xu Yuanqing killed the official who had killed his father, then surrendered. The court faced a difficult question: should it punish him for taking a life, or honor him for fulfilling a son's duty?

One adviser, Chen Zi'ang, proposed doing both. About a century later, Liu Zongyuan challenged that answer by asking what had happened to the father in the first place. Through their disagreement, this episode of Reasoned Talk explores the Tang legal system, Confucian family duties, and the state's claim to administer justice. What does obedience to the law require when the people enforcing it may themselves have committed an injustice?

Hi, I'm Mason Hu, a lawyer in China. This is Reasoned Talk, a podcast about legal history in China and the West.

Sources and reading

Texts and links checked on October 24, 2026. Classical Chinese passages are paraphrased in English for this script; the English wording is not presented as a quotation from a published translation.

  • The narrative and its limits: New Book of Tang, volume 195, entry on Xu Yuanqing. The entry supplies the father's name, Zhao's county office and later role as a censor, the relay-station employment, the killing, surrender, and the ruler's wish to spare Xu. It reports contemporary approval of Chen's argument rather than giving a separate, detailed record of an execution or formal honors. The script therefore distinguishes the recommendation from an independently documented implementation.

  • Chen's argument: Chen Zi'ang, “Memorial on Revenge” (復讎議狀). The argument addresses family retaliation, the public prohibition on killing, sacrifice, punishment, and formal commendation. “Memorial on Revenge” is the descriptive English title used here; other translations occur.

  • Liu's reply: Liu Zongyuan, “Refutation of the Argument on Revenge” (駁復讎議), especially the alternatives beginning 若元慶之父 and 其或元慶之父. These are conditional arguments, not findings that Xu's father was innocent or that officials suppressed his family's complaints. The text also explains why lawful punishment does not create a legitimate family claim to revenge.

  • Revenge in the ritual tradition: Book of Rites, “Tan Gong,” Chinese text with translation and commentary by Robert Eno (2016), section 3.47, printed pp. 55–56. The passage concerns a child's duty toward a parent's enemy; the accompanying note also reproduces the “same sky” formulation from “Qu Li, Part One.” The script paraphrases the classical image rather than quoting Eno's English translation. Liu's qualifications should be read alongside that forceful expression of duty.

  • Family duties within the Code: Tang Code with Commentaries, volume 1, “Ten Abominations”, especially 不孝 and 不義; and Columbia University's English selections from Article 6, translated in Sources of Chinese Tradition, second edition, volume 1, pp. 549–552. The script does not infer that killing any censor automatically constituted the particular offense of 不義; that category depended on specified relationships and circumstances.

  • Planned killing and official accountability: Tang Code, volume 17, provision 256, 謀殺人; volume 29, interrogation provisions; and volume 30, provisions 485, 487, and 497, on reporting requirements, wrongful imposition of criminal liability, and approval before execution. The Code provides institutional context; it does not supply a surviving judgment identifying the precise provision applied in Xu's case.

  • Central judicial administration: Six Compendia of the Tang (唐六典), volume 18, Court of Judicial Review, including the explanation of adjudication and referral to the Ministry of Punishments; and volume 13, Censorate, on investigating officials and hearing grievances. This eighth-century institutional account is used for broad context, not as a record of the route taken by Xu's case. Office names and responsibilities changed over the dynasty.

  • Limits of the modern comparison: Leslie Green and Thomas Adams, “Legal Positivism,” Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, introduction and section 4. Legal validity, moral evaluation, and a duty to obey are distinct questions. The comparison in the script is an interpretive aid, not a claim that Chen or Liu belonged to a modern jurisprudential school.

In late seventh-century China, Xu Yuanqing killed the official who had killed his father, then surrendered. The court faced a difficult question: should it punish him for taking a life, or honor him for fulfilling a son's duty?

One adviser, Chen Zi'ang, proposed doing both. About a century later, Liu Zongyuan challenged that answer by asking what had happened to the father in the first place. Through their disagreement, this episode of Reasoned Talk explores the Tang legal system, Confucian family duties, and the state's claim to administer justice. What does obedience to the law require when the people enforcing it may themselves have committed an injustice?

Hi, I'm Mason Hu, a lawyer in China. This is Reasoned Talk, a podcast about legal history in China and the West.

Sources and reading

Texts and links checked on October 24, 2026. Classical Chinese passages are paraphrased in English for this script; the English wording is not presented as a quotation from a published translation.

  • The narrative and its limits: New Book of Tang, volume 195, entry on Xu Yuanqing. The entry supplies the father's name, Zhao's county office and later role as a censor, the relay-station employment, the killing, surrender, and the ruler's wish to spare Xu. It reports contemporary approval of Chen's argument rather than giving a separate, detailed record of an execution or formal honors. The script therefore distinguishes the recommendation from an independently documented implementation.

  • Chen's argument: Chen Zi'ang, “Memorial on Revenge” (復讎議狀). The argument addresses family retaliation, the public prohibition on killing, sacrifice, punishment, and formal commendation. “Memorial on Revenge” is the descriptive English title used here; other translations occur.

  • Liu's reply: Liu Zongyuan, “Refutation of the Argument on Revenge” (駁復讎議), especially the alternatives beginning 若元慶之父 and 其或元慶之父. These are conditional arguments, not findings that Xu's father was innocent or that officials suppressed his family's complaints. The text also explains why lawful punishment does not create a legitimate family claim to revenge.

  • Revenge in the ritual tradition: Book of Rites, “Tan Gong,” Chinese text with translation and commentary by Robert Eno (2016), section 3.47, printed pp. 55–56. The passage concerns a child's duty toward a parent's enemy; the accompanying note also reproduces the “same sky” formulation from “Qu Li, Part One.” The script paraphrases the classical image rather than quoting Eno's English translation. Liu's qualifications should be read alongside that forceful expression of duty.

  • Family duties within the Code: Tang Code with Commentaries, volume 1, “Ten Abominations”, especially 不孝 and 不義; and Columbia University's English selections from Article 6, translated in Sources of Chinese Tradition, second edition, volume 1, pp. 549–552. item.title: 01 From China to Europe: State Power and the Rule of Law
item.description:
In 221 BCE, Qin unified China under an emperor and a centralized administration. More than a thousand years later, scholars in medieval Bologna were studying Roman legal texts that would help shape Europe's legal institutions. How did the ability to govern develop alongside the idea that rulers themselves should be bound by law?

The first episode of Reasoned Talk takes Francis Fukuyama's The Origins of Political Order as a starting point. Moving from Qin's statutes and administrative practices to Justinian's compilation, medieval jurists, and natural law, it examines the relationship between state power and legal limits. What gives law the authority to constrain the people who govern?

Hi, I'm Mason Hu, a lawyer in China. This is Reasoned Talk, a podcast about legal history in China and the West.

Terms and names

  • Francis Fukuyama — The political scientist whose comparative framework guides this episode. His three institutions are the state, the rule of law, and accountable government.

  • State capacity — The ability of public institutions to implement decisions. It concerns administrative effectiveness, which should be distinguished from the extent of a ruler's powers.

  • Rule of law — Used here in Fukuyama's sense of law binding rulers themselves. Possessing a written code is insufficient to establish it.

  • Accountable government — Government that must answer to the governed. Democratic elections are a major modern mechanism of accountability.

  • Qin The First Emperor (秦始皇) — The First Emperor of China, whose state completed the conquest of its six major rivals in 221 BCE.

  • Shang Yang (商鞅) — The fourth-century BCE reformer associated with 秦's military and administrative reforms.

  • Li Kui (李悝)；Canon of Laws《法经》 — The traditional attribution and Chinese title of the lost Canon of Laws. The account of its six chapters comes from later sources.

  • Lv (律) and Ling (令) — Commonly translated as statutes and ordinances. “Orders” is also used for 令.

  • 《法律答问》 — Answers to Questions Concerning Qin Statutes. English translations of the title vary.

  • 《封诊式》 — Models for Sealing and Investigating. A collection of procedural models, rather than a modern code of procedure.

  • 廷行事 — Court practice, often discussed in connection with precedents. The term should not be taken to imply the modern common-law doctrine of binding precedent.

  • Corpus Iuris Civilis — The collective name for Justinian's legal compilation: the Institutes, Digest, Code, and Novels. Corpus Juris Civilis is an alternative spelling. The Code is one component of the collection.

  • Glossators — Medieval scholars who studied Roman legal texts through explanatory notes called glosses.

  • Canon law — The law of the Church; distinct from Roman civil law.

  • Thomas Aquinas; natural law — The thirteenth-century theologian connected human law with reason, the common good, and a Christian account of eternal law.
